title: Stagger and choreograph motion like nature
principle: Nature rarely moves in perfect synchrony—schools of fish and flocks of birds have slight timing differences. Rauno Freiberg’s Designing Depth extends this to UI: choreograph discrete states over a gesture, stagger sibling reveals, and reverse choreography based on where the trigger sits so motion teaches layering instead of feeling like a single keyframed pop.
procedure: Deconstruct the interaction into discrete states tied to the gesture (not one monolithic keyframe).
Prioritize motion near the trigger location first so the interface feels like it heard the user.
Stagger sibling items that look alike (grids, icon rows) with slight delays—enough to read as depth, not enough to feel slow.
When the same overlay can open from different triggers, reverse or retune choreography to match each origin.
Honor prefers-reduced-motion: collapse stagger to opacity-only or instant.
examplePrompts:
Rewrite this enter animation as a choreographed sequence (Rauno / Designing Depth):
- List 3–4 discrete states tied to the user gesture.
- Stagger sibling cards ≤40ms apart so the grid does not pop as one slab.
- Start motion nearest the click/focus origin.
- Keep total under ~300ms; transform+opacity only.
- Add prefers-reduced-motion fallback (opacity only or none).
Explain each state’s job in one line.
This list fades in all at once and feels fake. Stagger item opacity/translate like a flock takeoff—subtle, nature-timed—without making the page feel slower. Return CSS/WAAPI timings.
promptWhy: Discrete states + origin-first motion stops the model from shipping one generic fade-in keyframe.
Named stagger budget and reduced-motion keep craft from becoming sluggish decoration.
tips: OpenAI-style staggered grid fades add depth without feeling slower—users can tell what updated.
iPhone unlock staggers Home Screen apps to make a swipe feel three-dimensional.
iPad Dock sliding away vs blurring with Control Centre communicates different layer metaphors—match motion to affordance.

workedExamples.title: Home Screen swipe vs Search tap
workedExamples.before: Same overlay always plays one canned keyframe regardless of how you opened it.
workedExamples.after: Swipe-down prioritizes top-of-screen feedback then suggestions; tap-Search reverses—input morphs first near the footer trigger, suggestions slightly delayed.
workedExamples.body: Rauno documents iOS Search choreography differing by gesture origin. Choreography teaches where attention should go. Cite: rauno.me/craft/depth.

workedExamples.title: Staggered grid load
workedExamples.body: Sibling cards that appear in perfect sync feel synthetic. Slight stagger (inspired by natural flocks / OpenAI grid examples in the essay) clarifies how many items arrived and adds motion depth without adding wait.

workedExamples.title: Failure: stagger as delay tax
workedExamples.body: If staggered reveals push perceived wait past ~300ms or block keyboard-driven actions, delete the stagger. Depth never outranks responsiveness.

antiPatterns: One keyframed pop for every enter, ignoring gesture origin.
Long cascading delays that make the UI feel laggy.
checklist: Interaction broken into named states, not one blob animation.
Sibling stagger is subtle and timed under a responsive budget.

stateRequirements.responsive: Check 390px and desktop plus 200% zoom; preserve reading order, wrap long text and keep actions reachable.
stateRequirements.accessibility: Use semantic headings and native controls, visible labels and focus; normal text contrast at least 4.5:1.
stateRequirements.keyboard: Complete the primary action using Tab, Shift+Tab, Enter and Space; no pointer-only information or focus trap.
stateRequirements.reducedMotion: Remove nonessential movement; preserve all state and information without waiting for animation.
stateRequirements.loading: Show pending feedback only during real work; retain context and allow navigation away.
stateRequirements.empty: Distinguish no content from no matching results; explain how to proceed or reset filters.
stateRequirements.error: Explain the failed action, retain user input and offer recovery; never claim success on failure.
stateRequirements.interruption: A newer action wins; cancel or ignore stale results and keep controls responsive.
stateRequirements.stateChange: Announce important results politely without moving focus unexpectedly.

compatibility.rule: Start with one technique. Add at most one companion for a distinct unsolved problem; candidates are suggestions, not verified compatibility.
conflicts: Two techniques changing the same visual role require an explicit winner.
Do not combine multiple entrance or attention effects on one target.
Aesthetic subtraction must not remove semantics, feedback or attribution.
compatibility.stop: Stop when the named task is clearer and acceptance evidence is recorded; do not add polish without a problem.
